title: Bucking the trend
caption: The elliptical galaxy Messier 59 (NGC 4621), imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: Ranked #76 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A glowing, rounded ball of light fills this Hubble image. It is the galaxy NGC 4621, more familiar as Messier 59, photographed with the Advanced Camera for Surveys. It lies about 50 million light-years away in the Virgo Cluster, a gathering of some 2000 galaxies in the constellation Virgo, the Virgin.

Modern observations show Messier 59 is an elliptical, one of the three main kinds of galaxy alongside spirals and irregulars. Ellipticals are usually the most mature of the three, full of old red stars and forming few or no new ones.

Messier 59 partly breaks that pattern. It shows signs of star formation, with some newborn stars living in a disc close to its core. Finding young stars there shows that even galaxies dominated by old stars can still hold pockets of fresh activity.
scale: Messier 59 lies approximately 50 million light-years away, according to ESA/Hubble.

understand.summary: Hubble's ACS and WFPC2 observed in visible and near-infrared light. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal far more of the galaxy's glow than an eye could.

explore: The French comet hunter Charles Messier added the galaxy to his famous catalog of deep-sky objects, which is where its better-known name comes from. However, credit for its discovery goes to the German astronomer Johann Gottfried Koehler, who found it just days before Messier listed it.
